doc.title: Don Alias interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 6, 2002

chapter: Early life and path to music
title: His mother's reaction to his career change
summary: His mother wanted him to be a doctor and was upset he quit; she liked that he played with Miles Davis and Lou Rawls more than the music itself.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Well I’m wondering what the phone call to your mother was like when you decided to switch careers.

Hell. That’s the only thing, for want of a better word. Take into consideration the time. It was the sixties, the fifties and sixties. I’m a black American growing up in a certain kind of environment and the revolution wasn’t really going on when I was going to school, I’m talking about ’58, ’59. It wasn’t really prevalent then. There were no revolutionary activities around that time. Parents wanted their kids — I’m talking about Afro-American parents — wanted their kids to be doctors, lawyers, something with some kind of clout to it, intellectually, you know, clout to it. Stuff like that. And needless to say when I told her that I had quit my laboratory job she didn’t like that. As a matter of fact it was only recently, when I say recently I’m talking about maybe seven years maybe, that she — I think she liked more the people I was playing with than the playing. I said “Mom I’m playing with Miles Davis.” “Oh Miles Davis.” “Lou Rawls.” “Oh Lou Rawls, oh.” She would love all of that. But me being a musician, no she didn’t want that. She was really upset about that.
Gosh well she can at least brag to her neighbors perhaps.

She did that. She did do that. Because I’d be there on a number of occasions when she’d turn around — “oh he played with —” moms, you know. But she would never of course give me the credit. That’s all right, I accept it.
